title: Ang 488: Farid in Asa
hook: love from the heart closes the raga
tomorrow: what if your own mind were the grinding stone?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandalwood: Ravidas the castor plant, carrying a scent he didn't make, and Dhanna hearing a weaver's and a barber's names. Now, the last voice in Asa.

People argue about the last song on an album more than the first. It's the one you walk out humming. The raga of Asa runs on for page after page of the Gurus' hymns, then the Bhagats. And on ang 488, the very last word goes to a Sufi, Shaykh Farid, speaking of Allah and the grave. A Muslim saint closes a raga of the Sikh scripture. So here's the puzzle: why him?
screen: `THE LAST SONG ON THE ALBUM.` → `A SUFI CLOSES ASA.` → `WHY HIM?`

segments.voice: Start with what he says. In paraphrase: those who love from the heart are the true ones. Those with one thing in the mind and another on the lips are counted false. That's Farid's whole test, and notice what's missing from it: any label at all. No question of which community, which name, which door. Just this: does the inside match the outside? Then he goes on. Those dyed in love for the Lord delight in seeing him; those who forget the Name are a weight on the earth. In his second hymn he names himself, Shaykh Farid, and tells his dear one to hold on to Allah, because this body will turn to dust. So, the puzzle, solved. The Granth doesn't sort its singers by the door they came in. It sorts them the way Farid sorts people: is the love real all the way through? Farid says Allah. The Gurus say Hari, Gobind, the True One. The Granth sets them on the same pages, and Sikhs bow to the whole book. One small word to tap in his line: dil, the heart. Not the part of you that argues; the part that loves. Asa ends on it.
screen: `LOVE FROM THE HEART IS TRUE.` · `ONE THING INSIDE, ANOTHER OUTSIDE.` · `HOLD ON; THE BODY TURNS TO DUST.` · `SORTED BY THE HEART, NOT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `FROM THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper, and write Farid's test in your own hand: the inside the same as the outside. Set the pen down and leave the words in front of you for the sit, eyes resting on them. If you'd like to see his lines first, they're on ang 488.
Ang 488. The last page of Asa, where Shaykh Farid says the true ones are those who love from the heart.
From the heart: Farid's whole test, the inside matching the outside. Fifteen hundred days, and counting.

screen: `DAY 1500 COUNTS.` → `A WALK THROUGH THE GRANTH · 54 OF 180.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT IF YOUR MIND WERE THE GRINDING STONE?`

howItsDone: Shaykh Farid's hymns and saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras like the rest of the Granth; in Asa his two hymns are the raga's last, after the other Bhagats.

myth: Farid's hymns in the Granth use the name Allah
in his second hymn he tells his dear one to hold on to Allah.
Farid's test is about which community you belong to
his test is the heart: one thing inside and another on the lips is counted false.
in Farid's line, dil means the thinking mind
dil is the heart, the part that loves.

fork.setup: you're picking a volunteer lead. one has a perfect resume and talks about it a lot. one says little and keeps showing up. by Farid's test, what are you looking for?
options: whether what each one says matches what they do.
the stronger resume; it proves real commitment.
the quiet one; talking about it means it's fake.
fork.reveal: Farid's test isn't loud or quiet. it's the match: one thing in the mind and another on the lips is what he calls false.

original.note: Gurmukhi: dilhu muhabbat, love from the heart; Farid's opening on ang 488.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scripture holds only its own community's voices.
what it means: Asa closes with Shaykh Farid, a Sufi, whose test is love from the heart, not a label.
what a scholar hears: dilhu muhabbat jinh seee sachiaa, ang 488; scholars discuss whether these verses are the early Sufi Baba Farid's or a later shaykh's in his line.
guess: the page where Farid's hymns close the raga of Asa
the page where Guru Nanak's hymns open the raga of Gujri
a page of Kabir's sayings about love and death

chat.says: jas wants to film us serving at the table for his page. is that fake or am i being petty
options: Farid's test is inside matching outside. You can't see his heart, only yours.
Fake. Anything posted online can't come from the heart, so tell him no.
Fine either way; what counts is the food gets served, not anyone's why.
chat.meaning: Farid: those who love from the heart are true; one thing inside and another outside is false. The test is the heart, and you only see your own.

Farid.meaning: Shaykh Farid, a Sufi whose hymns close Asa

Sufi.meaning: a Muslim mystic, devoted to the love of God

Hari.meaning: a name for God the Gurus use

sources.ref: Ang 488 (Asa, Shaykh Farid, first hymn: dilhu muhabbat jinh seee sachiaa; jinh man hor mukh hor si kaandhe kachiaa), paraphrased
